title: A history worth reading
briefing: One commit isn't a history. In ~/tool there's a script, tool.sh. Get it
under git, then make a real change and commit that too — so the log shows
the story of how the file evolved.
End with two commits and a clean working tree.
tips: The everyday loop: edit a file → git add it → git commit. Repeat.
`git log` (or `git log --oneline`) shows the commits you've made, newest first.
objective: In a new ~/tool repo, commit tool.sh, then make a change to it and commit again — two commits, working tree clean.
expert_objective: Give ~/tool a two-commit history with a clean tree.
hints: First commit: `cd ~/tool && git init && git add tool.sh && git commit -m "first version"`.
Change the file, then commit again: append a line with `echo ... >> tool.sh`, then `git add tool.sh` and `git commit -m "..."`.
`echo 'echo done' >> tool.sh`, then `git commit -am "print done when finished"` (‑a stages the tracked change). `git log --oneline` shows two commits.
solution:
cd ~/tool
git init
git add tool.sh
git commit -m "first version"
echo 'echo done' >> tool.sh
git commit -am "print done when finished"
git log --oneline
explanation: This is the loop you'll run thousands of times: change something, `git add`, `git commit`. Each commit is a labelled snapshot you can return to, and `git log` reads back the story. `git commit -a` is a shortcut that stages changes to already-tracked files for you.
